newsitem.title: FALKLAND ISLANDS: FEATURE - Falklanders see their future in oil.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Falklanders see their future in oil.

text.p: The Falkland Islands, one of the last scraps of the British Empire, are betting there is oil under their stormy waters and that it will give them something they badly need: a future.

With Argentina still maintaining its claim on the islands 15 years after invading them, the Falklands have about one British soldier for every resident and a huge military base that can bring in thousands more troops overnight.
They have prosperity and self-sufficiency thanks to the sale of fishing licenses to foreign fleets, a promise from Britain never to leave and growing economic links with Chile.

Now the 2,000 people living on these stark, windswept islands with about a million sheep hope oil will bring them real economic security for the future and let them shed their image as a colonial curiosity.
''We have a good standard of living at the moment,'' said Phyllis Rendell, director of oil for the Falkland Islands government.

''But if fish stocks collapsed next year, we'd be ruined. We'd have to go back to Britain for a handout and we can't have that,'' she said in a Port Stanley pub, where the English accents and lager can make you forget you're only 200 miles from the coast of South America.

Last October the islands accepted bids from five international consortia, including big foreign names like Royal Dutch/Shell and International Petroleum, to gather seismic data in seven offshore tracts north of the islands.

Depending on the results of the seismic surveys, exploratory drilling could start as early as late 1997, local officials said. No one knows how much oil there is but analysts have spoken of two billion to three billion barrels, based on preliminary seismic data.

''The prospecting data seem to be good,'' said the islands' London-appointed governor Richard Ralph. ''The oil companies are obviously interested enough to invest in a quite significant way in the exploration phase.''
GETTING RICH OFF SQUID

But even before the first well is sunk, life is changing fast in the Falklands. Low prices are killing the traditional wool industry and so, like other island states around the world, the Falklands have grown rich selling fishing licenses to big foreign fleets that want to trawl.
Ships from Taiwan to Poland haul in tonnes of ilex squid, and the Falklands treasury hauls in the millions of pounds they pay in fishing rights.

Four-wheel-drive vehicles rumble down the islands' rocky roads, nearly all households have television, and Port Stanley, the capital, has a new hospital and a gleaming new school complete with swimming pool.
Children living on remote sheep ranches in "the camp," as the countryside is known here, have a daily radio linkup with school in Port Stanley.

The British military have built a modern airport on the site where a lonely shepherd's house once stood, and the ride into Port Stanley, which used to take up to eight hours over bogs and hills, now takes 45 minutes.
There's a weekly commercial air flight on a Boeing 727 to Punta Arenas, Chile, and well-stocked, if expensive, shops.
"WE'RE A MODERN SOCIETY"
It's all a long way from the neglected backwater of before 1982, when Argentina, acting on a long-standing sovereignty claim, invaded the islands and renamed the capital Puerto Argentino.
"It was all rather backward before the war. Communications were difficult, farming was done in the old traditional way," Ralph told Reuters.

"Today we're becoming a modern society, with all the benefits that go with that. There's real prosperity. People travel, go for holidays in Florida or the south of France. We've got TV, we've got a very fast-growing network of roads," he said. "And we have no lack of funds thanks to the sale of fishing licenses."
But Falklanders seem uneasy about leaving their fate to squid, especially seeing how the bottom dropped out of wool.
"Look what's happened to fish stocks all over the world. The fish could run out any time and then we're really finished," said one resident.

Oil, if any is found, would make the well-heeled Falklands an even wealthier place. The islands' government has offered to pay Britain its annual defence costs of about 65 million pounds ($110 million) from oil revenues.
ARGENTINA COOPERATES
Argentina, which calls the islands the Islas Malvinas, is also seeking a three percent royalty payment on any oil produced.

Some Falklanders view the prospect of oil uneasily, worrying it will mean the end of their rural way of life, bring swarms of grubby foreign oil workers and turn the islands into little more than an offshore oil platform with penguins.

"We've got this very progressive, go-ahead business community now that wants to make money at any cost, and then there are people who don't want anything to change," said Rendell. "Opinions tend to be very polarised."

Trying to be sensitive to local concerns, the government has ordered seismic work to stop for four months from February 1 because natives area worried it would disturb the squid during breeding season.
Argentina, trying a more conciliatory tack to regain the islands recently, has cooperated at every step, officials said.

In 1995 Argentina and Britain signed an agreement on safety, environmental and logistical issues associated with oil. But the pact's real significance was to show Argentina would not use its sovereignty claim to try to stop oil drilling, officials said.
"The agreement sent a clear signal to oil companies that the sovereignty issue is not going to intrude. That was very reassuring," said Ralph.
Buenos Aires, London and the Falklands government are now in three-way talks to allow oil exploration in an area southwest of the islands.
Exploration licenses for that area, known as the Special Cooperation Area, could be granted in 1998 and would mark an even greater milestone in rapprochement with Argentina, officials said.
"Oil companies, particularly the American ones, want to see dialogue with Argentina," said Rendell. "They want to feel they can put their money into a place that's not going to blow up tomorrow."
